summary: Defines a MIME content type that a mail transfer agent or gateway can use to report the outcome of trying to deliver a message to one or more recipients. It was replaced by RFC 3464.

plainLanguage.summary: When a mail server cannot deliver a message, it normally sends a note back to the sender. This RFC gives that note a standard layout so that mail programs can read it instead of guessing at the wording. The note says which server is reporting, and then says, for each recipient, what happened and why.

subtitle: A standard, machine-readable format for a mail server to report what happened to a message it tried to deliver.

tldr.problem: Mail systems used several different, mostly human-readable formats for bounce messages, so a program could not reliably tell what went wrong with a delivery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIME content type, message/delivery-status, carried inside multipart/report, with a set of per-message fields naming the reporting server and a group of per-recipient fields giving the address, the action taken and a transport-independent status code.
tldr.outcome: Reports became uniform enough for mail programs to read, including reports translated from other mail systems through a gateway. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 3464 and updated by RFC 2852.

facts.label: Status code shape
facts.value: Three numbers separated by dots, e.g. 5.0.0

facts.label: Status first number
facts.value: 2 = success, 4 = persistent temporary failure, 5 = permanent failure

today: RFC 1894 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3464 and updated by RFC 2852, so read those for the current rules.

sections.title: What a Delivery Status Notification Is For
sections.content:
This RFC defines a MIME content type that a message transfer agent (MTA) or electronic mail gateway can use to report the result of an attempt to deliver a message to one or more recipients. The content type is intended as a machine-processable replacement for the various types of delivery status notification used in Internet electronic mail, and it is meant to be used inside the multipart/report content type.

The memo lists the purposes such a report should serve: telling a person what happened to a message and why it failed, in a way that does not depend on any human language; letting a mail user agent match a returned report to the message it sent; letting mailing list exploders keep their subscriber lists up to date when delivery fails repeatedly; carrying delivery and non-delivery reports that come from foreign mail systems through a gateway; and giving the maintainer of a remote MTA enough information to understand a reported error.

Because the same report has to serve all of these audiences, the format carries both the original and the final form of a recipient address, and both a transport-independent and a transport-specific delivery status.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC gives the bounce message that mail servers send a standard layout, so that a program can read it. The layout also survives the trip between different kinds of mail system.

sections.title: The Four Mail Transfer Agents
sections.content:
A message often passes through several message transfer agents before it reaches a recipient, and recipient addresses may be rewritten along the way, so each agent may see a different form of the address. The RFC therefore gives the agents fixed names, and several DSN fields are defined in terms of the view from one of them.

  • The Original MTA is the one to which the sender submits the message for delivery.
  • The Received-From MTA is the MTA from which the Reporting MTA received the message and accepted responsibility for delivering it.
  • The Reporting MTA is the one reporting the results of the delivery attempts described in the report. It is always the agent that attempted the delivery, relay or gateway operation.
  • The Remote MTA is the next-hop MTA that the Reporting MTA could not hand the message to, or that refused to accept responsibility for some of its recipients.

The Reporting-MTA field is required in every DSN. The Reporting MTA is not necessarily the MTA that actually issued the DSN: if an attempt to deliver a message outside the Internet produced a non-delivery notification that was then gatewayed back into Internet mail, the Reporting-MTA field names the MTA that originally reported the failure, not the gateway that converted it into a DSN.
sections.plainLanguage: Four agents get names: the one the sender handed the message to, the one that passed it on, the one that tried to deliver it, and the one on the far side that refused it. Each field in the report says which of them it is talking about.

sections.title: The message/delivery-status Content Type
sections.content:
A DSN is a MIME message whose top-level content type is multipart/report. The report-type parameter is delivery-status. The first component of the multipart/report holds a human-readable explanation, the second is of content type message/delivery-status, and, if the original message or part of it is to be returned to the sender, it appears as the third component.

The body of the message/delivery-status part consists of one or more fields formatted according to the ABNF of RFC 822 header fields. The per-message fields appear first, followed by a blank line, and then one or more groups of per-recipient fields, each group preceded by a blank line: delivery-status-content = per-message-fields 1*( CRLF per-recipient-fields ).

The per-message fields are the optional Original-Envelope-Id, the required Reporting-MTA, the optional DSN-Gateway, the optional Received-From-MTA, the optional Arrival-Date, and any number of extension fields. The per-recipient fields are the optional Original-Recipient, the required Final-Recipient, the required Action, the required Status, and the optional Remote-MTA, Diagnostic-Code, Last-Attempt-Date and Will-Retry-Until, followed by any number of extension fields.

Several fields carry a -type subfield before their value: an address-type that says how to read a mailbox address, a diagnostic-type that says how to read a status code, and an MTA-name-type that says how to read an agent name. Internet mail addresses use the rfc822 address-type, SMTP reply codes use smtp, and a host's domain name uses dns.
sections.plainLanguage: The report has two halves. The first names the server that is reporting and, when it applies, the gateway that translated the report. The second repeats one block per recipient, and each block names the address and says what happened to it.

sections.title: Per-Recipient Fields and Action Values
sections.content:
The Final-Recipient field names the recipient the block applies to, and MUST be present in every block. It holds the address as it was when the message was accepted for delivery by the Reporting MTA, with the case of alphabetic characters preserved. The optional Original-Recipient field holds the address the sender originally specified, so that a sender can match the report against its own records.

The Action field says what the Reporting MTA did with the message, and MUST be present for each recipient. It takes one of five values: failed, meaning the agent has abandoned its attempts and no further notice is expected; delayed, meaning it will keep trying and more notices may follow; delivered, meaning the message reached the address the sender specified, which is a terminal state and does not mean it was read; relayed, meaning the message was passed into an environment that does not accept responsibility for reporting successful delivery; and expanded, meaning it was delivered to the sender's address and then forwarded beyond it to several more addresses, which is not a terminal state.

The Status field carries a transport-independent status code made of three numbers separated by dots. The first number says whether the attempt succeeded (2), failed in a way that may be temporary (4), or failed permanently (5). The second points to the probable source of the problem and the third gives a precise error condition if one is known. The optional Diagnostic-Code field keeps the original, transport-specific code, which translation into the transport-independent form may have lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Each recipient block says what happened to that recipient: failed, delayed, delivered, relayed or expanded. A separate status number then says whether the problem is temporary or permanent, in a form that means the same thing in every mail system.

sections.title: Conformance and Usage Requirements
sections.content:
An MTA or gateway conforms to this specification if it generates DSNs according to the protocol defined here. For implementations that do not support requests for positive delivery notification, it is sufficient that delivery failure reports use this protocol.

A minimal implementation need generate only the Reporting-MTA per-message field, and the Final-Recipient, Action and Status fields for each attempt to deliver a message to a recipient described by the DSN. Generation of the other fields, when appropriate, is strongly recommended. MTAs and gateways MUST NOT generate the Original-Recipient field unless the mail transfer protocol provides the address originally specified by the sender at the time of submission, because ordinary SMTP does not make that guarantee.

Each sender-specified recipient address SHOULD result in at most one delivered or failed DSN for that recipient. Successful submission of a message to a mailing list exploder is considered final delivery, and the Reporting MTA SHOULD issue an appropriate DSN exactly as if the recipient address were an ordinary mailbox. That is what lets a list exploder catch non-delivery reports and drop addresses that keep failing.
sections.plainLanguage: An implementation only has to write four kinds of field to conform: which server is reporting, and for each recipient the address, what happened and the status. The remaining fields are worth adding whenever the information is available.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DSNs may be forged as easily as ordinary Internet electronic mail. A forged report can claim that a message was delivered when it was not, or that it failed when it did arrive, or name a false Final-Recipient or Remote-MTA, or arrive unsolicited. User agents and automatic mail handling facilities that act on DSNs should take appropriate precautions to minimise the potential damage from denial-of-service attacks.

Confidentiality is the other dimension. A recipient who forwards mail to a private address may not want that address disclosed, and the RFC lists several ways an MTA can protect it, including issuing a relayed DSN instead of a detailed one, omitting the Remote and extension fields that would otherwise carry the confidential information, and setting the envelope return address to the NULL reverse-path so that no further reports reach the original sender.

Even a genuine failure report is not a guarantee that a message was not received. A race condition in SMTP allows messages to be duplicated if a connection drops after a completed DATA command but before the response is seen, so the client retransmits a message the server already has. If one of those attempts succeeds and the other fails, a failed DSN can be issued even though the message actually reached the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write a fake report, so a program that acts on reports automatically should check them first. A failure report also does not prove the message was never received: the mail protocol can send the same message twice, and one copy can succeed while the other is reported as failed.

messages.label: RELAY ATTEMPT
messages.note: The remote MTA refuses to take responsibility for the recipients.

messages.label: RETURN DSN
messages.note: The report goes back to the sender.

items.label: Failed
items.desc: The agent has stopped trying to deliver to this recipient. No further notice is expected.

items.label: Delayed
items.desc: The agent will keep trying, and more notices may follow.

items.label: Delivered
items.desc: The message reached the address the sender specified. A terminal state, and it does not mean the message was read.

items.label: Relayed
items.desc: The message was passed into an environment that does not report successful delivery.

items.label: Expanded
items.desc: The message reached the sender's address and was forwarded beyond it to several more addresses. Not a terminal state.

data.title: DSN field layout
data.code:
per-message-fields =
     [ original-envelope-id-field CRLF ]
     reporting-mta-field CRLF
     [ dsn-gateway-field CRLF ]
     [ received-from-mta-field CRLF ]
     [ arrival-date-field CRLF ]
     *( extension-field CRLF )

per-recipient-fields =
     [ original-recipient-field CRLF ]
     final-recipient-field CRLF
     action-field CRLF
     status-field CRLF
     [ remote-mta-field CRLF ]
     [ diagnostic-code-field CRLF ]
     [ last-attempt-date-field CRLF ]
     [ will-retry-until-field CRLF ]
     *( extension-field CRLF )
